# Audio

Sound that arrives from, or leaves for, somewhere other than Field's own signal graph: analysis products written by an offline tool, the network protocols that carry control data, the Dirt sample library on disk, an Ableton Live set read off the filesystem, and Sonic Pi driven as an owned child process with no window of its own. `SoundPathMap.kt` is the one to read first: the declared, re-derived-from-the-code map of every route Field has from a box to something audible, which [Making a sound in Field: every path there is](../sound_paths.md) renders as a page. [Sonic Pi](../sonic_pi.md) covers owned mode in full.

77 source file(s), 2086 public symbol(s), 1004 of them carrying KDoc. Everything below is the documentation that lives beside the code — the same text the [completion documentation panel](../completion_doc_browser.md) shows in the editor. A blank summary means the declaration has no KDoc yet, not that this page dropped it.

## essentiaAnalysis.kt { #essentiaanalysis-kt }

Readers for two on-disk audio-analysis products, so a box can query them by time.

Nothing here performs analysis or links against a native library — both entry points just parse
files that some offline tool has already written.

`loadFramesSig` reads an Essentia-shaped YAML `.sig` file into a [`FramesSigDocument`](audio.md#essentiaanalysis-kt-framessigdocument): the tree is
flattened into dotted paths, and each leaf is sorted into a scalar, a per-frame
[`FramesSigFloatProduct`](audio.md#essentiaanalysis-kt-framessigfloatproduct), or a per-frame [`FramesSigFloatVectorProduct`](audio.md#essentiaanalysis-kt-framessigfloatvectorproduct). `sampleAt` /
`floatValueAt` / `floatVectorAt` map a time in seconds to a frame index by assuming frames are
evenly spaced across the analysis window described in `metadata` (`analysis.start_time` and
`analysis.length`, falling back to the audio length); `available` / `availableArrays` list what
a given file actually contains. Large `.sig` files are handled by raising SnakeYAML's code-point
limit to the file size plus padding.

`loadSound2Vec` reads a directory of `metadata.csv` + `embeddings.npy` (+ optional
`manifest.json`) into a [`Sound2VecDataset`](audio.md#essentiaanalysis-kt-sound2vecdataset) of [`Sound2VecClip`](audio.md#essentiaanalysis-kt-sound2vecclip)s, each carrying its embedding, its
time span within a source audio file, and optional t-SNE 2D/3D coordinates; clips can be looked
up by chunk id, or by audio path and time. The bundled `.npy` reader is narrow: it
accepts only C-ordered (non-Fortran) `float32` 1D or 2D arrays, and by default requires the CSV
row count, the embedding row count and the manifest's `num_chunks` / `embedding_dim` to agree.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/analysis/essentiaAnalysis.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/analysis/essentiaAnalysis/)

Distill both sounds against the same harmonic numbering first. `referenceLabel` names the partial whose frequency guides quiet partials (Loris's reference partial); 0 disables it. `amplitudeShape` is Loris's log-amplitude morph shape (0 keeps Loris's default). |

## AbletonLinkAudio.kt { #abletonlinkaudio-kt }

Ableton Link from inside Field: a tempo, beat and phase shared with every Link peer on the
network, and audio published to and taken from them.

[`LinkAudioInterface`](audio.md#abletonlinkaudio-kt-linkaudiointerface) is the whole surface and there is one of it per process. `shared` opens it
or hands back the one already open, `currentOrNull` asks whether there is one without opening
one, and `destroyShared` closes it so that the next `shared` builds a new one. Boxes usually
arrive through `abletonLink`, `linkTiming`, `linkAudioOut`, `linkAudioIn` and
`linkAudioInStereo` in `synth.kt`, none of which ask the caller for an interface.

The timing half is a session state every peer on the network shares. `setTempo`, `setPlaying`
and `requestBeat` write into it, `enableStartStopSync` decides whether transport start and stop
travel with it, and [`LinkTimingSnapshot`](audio.md#abletonlinkaudio-kt-linktimingsnapshot) is the read: tempo, beat, phase, peer count and Link's
own microsecond clock, all taken at one instant. [`FieldAudioEngine`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-fieldaudioengine) takes a snapshot per audio
block and hangs it on the [`SynthContext`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-synthcontext) every [`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal) renders against, which is where
`linkBeat`, `linkPhase` and `linkTempo` come from. [`ParamScope`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-paramscope) re-exposes the same values, so a
[`Param`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-param) expression can read them too.

The audio half is Link Audio, which carries sound between peers of that same session.
`enableAudioOutput` publishes a named channel and `FieldAudioEngine.enableLinkOutput` is what
points the mix at it; `channels` lists the channels the session is carrying, and `monoInput` and
`stereoInput` subscribe to one of them and hand back a [`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal) the graph uses like any other
source. Sonic Pi's `link_audio` reads a channel published this way, and
[Sonic Pi](../sonic_pi.md) covers that end of it, including the Link visibility setting that has
to be on before either side can see the other.

There are two `SessionState`s here because Link has two. One is captured and committed under a
lock for calls arriving from a box or the UI; the other is captured inside the audio block, so
that the beat the block starts on and the buffer rendered for it are committed together.
`linkAudioCommits`, `linkAudioCommitFailures` and `linkAudioInvalidBuffers` count how that goes,
and they are live-graph children along with the peer count and the channel list, so an open
interface can be walked by a live-graph query.

None of the Link bindings are Kotlin — `com.ableton.link` comes from `libs/ableton-link-ffm.jar`,
over a native Link library the build points at with the `ableton.link.library` system property.

## AbletonSet.kt { #abletonset-kt }

An Ableton Live set read into Field: tracks, clips, tempo, automation and sample analysis.

`AbletonSet.read` parses an `.als`, which is gzipped XML — recognised by its magic bytes rather
than its extension, so an already-unzipped set reads too. The model runs [`AbletonSet`](audio.md#abletonset-kt-abletonset) to
[`AbletonTrack`](audio.md#abletonset-kt-abletontrack) to [`AbletonClip`](audio.md#abletonset-kt-abletonclip), with [`AbletonTempoMap`](audio.md#abletonset-kt-abletontempomap) converting between arrangement beats and
seconds.

The queries take an arrangement position and answer for that instant:
`AbletonSet.clipsPlayingAtBeat`, `AbletonSet.trackVolumesAtBeat` and
`AbletonSet.dominantPitchesAtBeat`, each with an `AtSeconds` twin.
[`AbletonAutomationEnvelope`](audio.md#abletonset-kt-abletonautomationenvelope) carries the envelopes they read.

A clip names its audio through [`AbletonSampleRef`](audio.md#abletonset-kt-abletonsampleref), which [`AbletonSampleFileMapper`](audio.md#abletonset-kt-abletonsamplefilemapper) and
`AbletonSet.resolveSamples` resolve to files on this machine. Opening those files is what
[`AbletonSampleVolumeAnalysisCache`](audio.md#abletonset-kt-abletonsamplevolumeanalysiscache) and [`AbletonSamplePitchAnalysisCache`](audio.md#abletonset-kt-abletonsamplepitchanalysiscache) are for: both memoise
in process and on disk, keyed on the sample's path, size, modification time and the analysis
config, so a second run is a lookup rather than a re-read.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/AbletonSet.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/AbletonSet/)

## AbletonSetDebugDrawing.kt { #abletonsetdebugdrawing-kt }

An [`AbletonSet`](audio.md#abletonset-kt-abletonset) drawn as a timeline: a row of clip rectangles per track, an automation curve
under it per envelope, at a fixed number of pixels per beat.

`AbletonSet.toDebugFLines` is the call and returns a flat list of `FLine`s; `debugFLineMap` is
the same drawing under one key, for a box that publishes its lines as a map. Both take an
[`AbletonSetFLineDebugOptions`](audio.md#abletonsetdebugdrawing-kt-abletonsetflinedebugoptions) or a builder block, and `abletonSetFLineDebugOptions` builds one
on its own.

Geometry is beats times `pixelsPerBeat` along x and a stack of fixed-height lanes along y: a
track takes `clipLaneHeight` plus one `automationLaneHeight` per envelope it carries, with
`trackGap` between tracks. The drawing is at least sixteen beats wide however short the set is,
and `includeMainTrack` decides whether the set's main track is drawn beside its ordinary ones.
An envelope is sampled at `automationSamples` points across that width, and within its lane a
higher value sits at a smaller y, normalised by the envelope's declared range, falling back to
the spread of its own events, then to a unit interval around its manual value, then to 0 to 1.
`includeGuides` rules a line under each track's clip row and another under the track;
`markAutomationEvents` ticks each envelope event at its own time.

Colour comes from Live's track colour index into a palette of 32, with a golden-ratio hue as the
fallback for a track that has no index or a negative one, and a disabled clip is drawn at a
lower alpha rather than omitted. Every line carries `ableton.*` properties naming the track,
clip, envelope or event it was drawn from, so the picture can be queried as well as looked at.

There is no connection to a running Live here. The input is an [`AbletonSet`](audio.md#abletonset-kt-abletonset) parsed off disk, so
the drawing works on a machine that has never had Live installed.

## BandAnalysis.kt { #bandanalysis-kt }

Band energy from audio that is already playing: a bank of band-pass filters, and the RMS of what
each one passes.

[`BandSplit`](audio.md#bandanalysis-kt-bandsplit) is the bank and `logBands` builds one with log-spaced centres. Both read an
[`AudioSnapshot`](synthesis.md#visualizers-kt-audiosnapshot), a copy of what the audio path last produced, so a measurement never renders a
synth graph a second time. What comes back is one `Double` per band in the order the centres were
given, which is the shape a frame's worth of code can hand to a shader or a particle force.

    val launch = patSynth(stack(pat("bd*4"), pat("hh*16")), cps = 2.0)
    val split = logBands(4, lowHz = 70.0, highHz = 8000.0, sampleRate = launch.bank.sampleRate)
    val perFrame = launch.bank.sampleRate / 60
    frames {
        while (frame()) {
            launch.advanceOffline(perFrame)
            val energy = split.measure(launch.tap.snapshot())
            // energy[0] is the lowest band, and hears the kick; energy[3] is the highest, and
            // hears the hats
        }
    }

Something has to be pulling the bank, or the tap stays empty and every band reads zero. Above the
box pulls it, which measures without sounding and does not depend on there being an output
device; returning the launch as the box's last expression hands it to the audio engine instead,
which pulls it when there is a device to play it through. Doing both advances the voices twice.

Per band the reading is the RMS of the filtered window's second half, the first half being the
filters' settling. The filters keep their state between calls, so successive overlapping
snapshots read as a smoothed series rather than as independent measurements.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/BandAnalysis.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/BandAnalysis/)

## DirtRender.kt { #dirtrender-kt }

Offline rendering of a pattern through the **real** Dirt sample library.

The other renderer in this package, `patRenderStereo`, goes through `patVoice`: a sine for `bd`,
filtered white noise for `sd` and `hh`. That stand-in needs no assets, so it works in CI and on
a clean checkout. It also sounds like bursts of white noise, because it *is* bursts of white
noise. It is not the voice behind most of the published audio figures either:
[`DocsAudioProvenance`](audio.md#docsaudioprovenance-kt-docsaudioprovenance) resolves each published clip to the producer that rendered it,
`DocsAudioProvenanceGuardTest` pins the resulting corpus by count and by family, and
`public/docs/sound.md` states the mix in prose. The largest family comes from
[`DoughDspSoundDocs`](synthesis.md#doughdspsounddocs-kt-doughdspsounddocs), which never reaches the stand-in voice at all.

The genuine Tidal sample set was already playable, but only *live*: `playDirt` drives a
polyphonic [`DirtSamplePlayer`](audio.md#dirtsamples-kt-dirtsampleplayer) through `respondAhead`, a clock and an audio device, none of which
exist inside a docs build or a headless box run. Here the same library, loaded by `libraryOrNull`
from wherever `dirtSampleRoot` finds it, is mixed straight into a buffer, so a transcript, a docs
capture or a `println`-and-listen box can sound like actual drums with no audio device anywhere.

Fallback happens at two different granularities:

 * **No library on this machine** — the whole render falls back to `patRenderStereo`. Nothing
   breaks, the figures still generate, and `DirtRenderResult.usedSamples` is `false`, so a
   caller can say which one you are hearing.
 * **Library present, token missing from it** — only *that event* falls back to the synth voice.
   A pattern of note numbers, or one naming a drum Dirt has never heard of, must not go silent
   just because the library loaded.

Both are for a box, where something audible beats an error. A published clip wants the
opposite: `strict = true` turns either case into an exception, and the docs renderers pass
`DirtRender.requirePinnedLibrary`, the checksummed subset `./gradlew fetchDocsDirtSamples`
downloads, so a clip is made from the same bytes on every machine or not made at all.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/DirtRender.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/DirtRender/)

## DirtSamples.kt { #dirtsamples-kt }

The TidalCycles Dirt-Samples collection loaded, indexed, and played from Field.

`dirt` attaches a [`DirtSampleLibrary`](audio.md#dirtsamples-kt-dirtsamplelibrary) to the current box context and `dirtPlayer` builds a
polyphonic [`DirtSamplePlayer`](audio.md#dirtsamples-kt-dirtsampleplayer) from it; `PatPattern.playDirt` drives one from a pattern of
`family:variant` tokens. The library scans a directory into [`DirtSampleFamily`](audio.md#dirtsamples-kt-dirtsamplefamily) groups of
[`DirtSampleDescriptor`](audio.md#dirtsamples-kt-dirtsampledescriptor), each resolving to a [`StereoAudioSample`](audio.md#dirtsamples-kt-stereoaudiosample).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/DirtSamples.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/DirtSamples/)

**Used in:** [Boolean network music examples](../boolean_network_music_examples.md), [A Petri net that throws sparks](../chain_petri_sparks.md)

## DoughDspPlotGallery.kt { #doughdspplotgallery-kt }

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/DoughDspPlotGallery.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/DoughDspPlotGallery/)

### DoughDspPlotGallery { #doughdspplotgallery-kt-doughdspplotgallery }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">DoughDspPlotGallery</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/DoughDspPlotGallery/#L57)

Headless **response-gallery / plot-capture harness** for the dough DSP ports in `DoughDsp`. It is the visual companion to `DoughDspSmokeTest` (which asserts the same behaviour numerically): every plotted point comes from actually *running* a primitive on the CPU — an impulse into [`PlateReverb`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-platereverb), a swept sine into [`Phaser`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-phaser) / [`ChamberlinLowpass`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-chamberlinlowpass), a ramp into [`SoftDistort`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-softdistort), a gated [`CurvedADSR`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-curvedadsr), and raw [`ZawOsc`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-zawosc) / [`PulzeOsc`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-pulzeosc) periods — never a synthesized or hand-drawn curve.

| Declaration | Summary |

## FaustPolySoundDocs.kt { #faustpolysounddocs-kt }

The two published clips that make polyphony audible: one chord progression, eight voices and one.

`faust.md` describes a polyphonic instrument in prose, onset tables in samples and peak counts in
Hz; these two clips are the part of it a reader can listen to. The path renders offline with no
device, so [`DocsAudioProvenance`](audio.md#docsaudioprovenance-kt-docsaudioprovenance) re-renders both on every build and holds them against the
numbers this file asserts.

### Why the two clips differ only in `voices`

Polyphony cannot be demonstrated by a single clip. A recording of a chord and a recording of an
arpeggio sound different for reasons that have nothing to do with voices, so a reader has no way
to tell a voice bank from a well-chosen pattern. What cannot be explained away is **the same
notation, the same program and the same gain, rendered at `voices = 8` and at `voices = 1`**: the
notes are identical, so everything you can hear between them is voice allocation. At one voice
every note after the first steals the only voice there is, and that steal is audible:
`FaustVoiceBank.stealReleaseFrames` measures the click it costs.

This is the same demonstration the `faust_polyphony` starting point makes in its *three notes at
once* box, which is where the shape of it came from. That box displays its two renders as players
in its own output; these two fences are how the same comparison reaches the page.

### Why the voice is a single sawtooth

The program here is **not** the detuned pair the rest of `faust.md` uses. The starting point's
chord box records why: two sawtooths 0.5% apart put a *beating pair* into the band the count is
taken in, so four voices reported four peaks and one voice reported two — which muddies the only
thing the figure is for. A clip whose stated measurement is a peak count has to be a signal with
one partial per note.

### Why a peak in this band can only be a note

The smoke test counts spectral peaks between `BAND_LO_HZ` and `BAND_HI_HZ` during the first chord,
`[c4,ef4,g4]`. Its fundamentals are 130.81, 155.56 and 196.00 Hz and the lowest second harmonic in
the chord is 261.6 Hz, so nothing but a fundamental can appear in that band: counting peaks there
counts notes sounding. Eight voices must show three and one voice must show one, and the one-voice
render must report steals. Those are the assertions, and `faust.md` is required to carry both
captions verbatim, so its prose cannot drift off the audio it publishes.

## Midi.kt { #midi-kt }

A Standard MIDI File surface for Field.

`readMidiClip` reads a `.mid` into a [`MidiClip`](audio.md#midi-kt-midiclip) and `MidiClip.writeTo` writes one back as a
format-1 file; `Sequence.toMidiClip` converts a `javax.sound.midi.Sequence` already in hand.
`AbletonSet.kt` reads MIDI through this file rather than carrying its own helpers, so the
note-on to note-off pairing in `Sequence.readTimedNotes`, along with `Sequence.tempoEvents`
and `tickToSeconds`, lives here.

Time is carried in *beats* (quarter notes) in the Field-native model, because that is what the
pattern stack speaks. Ticks and PPQ are a file-format detail and appear only at the edges, in
[`MidiTempoEvent`](audio.md#midi-kt-miditempoevent), [`MidiTimedNote`](audio.md#midi-kt-miditimednote) and the reader and writer.

`MidiClip.quantized` and `MidiClip.transposed` return edited copies; `quantize` and `gridError`
snap and score a [`MidiNote`](audio.md#midi-kt-midinote) list against a beat grid, and [`GeneralMidi`](audio.md#midi-kt-generalmidi) holds the program
numbers and the percussion channel as named constants.

## MidiDevices.kt { #mididevices-kt }

Live MIDI device I/O, and offline rendering of a [`MidiClip`](audio.md#midi-kt-midiclip) to a WAV through the JDK's own
software synthesizer.

[`MidiDevices`](audio.md#mididevices-kt-mididevices) enumerates what the JVM can see and opens a [`MidiOutput`](audio.md#mididevices-kt-midioutput) or [`MidiInput`](audio.md#mididevices-kt-midiinput) on it;
`MidiClip.playTo` sends a clip to a device by name fragment. `MidiClip.renderWav` and
`renderToWav` take the offline route instead, which needs no hardware at all.

Everything here has to survive a machine with no MIDI hardware, so every entry point either
returns null or an empty list, or throws a message that names what was missing —
`midiRenderUnavailableReason` is that check on its own, for asking before committing to a
render. Nothing fakes a device.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/MidiDevices.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/MidiDevices/)

**Used in:** [SMPTE Timecode: LTC and MIDI Time Code](../smpte_timecode.md)

## MidiPat.kt { #midipat-kt }

The bridge between the pattern algebra and [`MidiClip`](audio.md#midi-kt-midiclip), plus a piano roll drawn as FLines.

Two vocabularies have to be reconciled, and the pattern stack's spelling wins both times.

**Cycles against beats.** A `PatPattern` is a function of *cycles*, measured in [`PatQ`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt-patq): a
rational over `BigInteger`, so a subdivision is exact however fine it gets. A MIDI file is
quarter notes and ticks. `beatsPerCycle` bridges the two, defaulting to 4 so that one cycle is
one bar of 4/4, which is what the mini-notation reads like. It is an `Int` because the import
direction divides by `ppq * beatsPerCycle`: an integer denominator is what lets `MidiClip.toPat`
rebuild every onset as an exact [`PatQ`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt-patq) rather than a truncated one. Export does not keep that
guarantee and cannot — [`MidiNote`](audio.md#midi-kt-midinote) holds its position as `Double` quarter notes.

**Velocity and channel are not in the Pat vocabulary.** `PatAlgebra.kt` names the parameters the
rest of the stack reads — `gain` for amplitude, conventionally 0..1, and `note` for MIDI pitch —
and there is no `velocity` parameter and no `channel`. Rather than add two more that only MIDI
would ever set, export reads velocity from `gain` when it is present, and from an explicit
`velocity` annotation (0..127) when a caller wants wire-level control. Import writes both, so a
round trip through the algebra keeps its dynamics either way; `MidiRoundTripTest.a pattern
exports to MIDI and comes back as a pattern` is where that is pinned.

A clip read back in becomes a *finite* pattern. Querying past the last note yields nothing
rather than looping, so reach for `slow`, `fast` or `cat` to place a clip inside a longer
structure.

**The piano roll** is FLine geometry rather than an SVG string: one filled rectangle per note
over a beat-and-bar grid, with a horizontal rule at every C to give the eye an octave reference
the way a real roll's keyboard gutter does. Each note line carries its pitch, velocity, start
beat and track index in `properties`, so a caller can hit-test a click back to the note it
landed on. Field's y axis grows *downward*, so a higher pitch draws at a smaller y; reversing
that yields an upside-down roll that still looks plausible.

## MidiSmokeTest.kt { #midismoketest-kt }

Smoke cover for the Standard MIDI File surface: writes a clip, reads it back, exports a pattern,
imports one, draws a roll, enumerates devices and opens a real output port.

It does **not** open a MIDI *input*, and cannot. Opening a CoreMIDI input spawns a non-daemon
`Java Sound MidiInDevice Thread` that survives both `Transmitter.close()` and
`MidiDevice.close()`, so a JVM that has opened one never exits naturally, and a `jvm-main` smoke
test is required to exit naturally. The live input loopback is covered by
`MidiRoundTripTest` instead, where Gradle tears the test JVM down regardless. See [`MidiInput`](audio.md#mididevices-kt-midiinput).

Everything is written to a temp directory that is deleted on the way out, so a run leaves no
files in the repository.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/MidiSmokeTest.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/MidiSmokeTest/)

## PatSpatialSoundDocs.kt { #patspatialsounddocs-kt }

Two of the published clips on `pat_spatial.md`: the **mono source**, before Steam Audio places it.

This is the half of the chain that needs nothing uncommitted: the pattern through one
[`DoughEngine`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughengine), taken as mono. It is the exact buffer [`PatSpatialRoom`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt-patspatialroom) copies into `source.mono`
and hands to [`afield.audio.spatial.steamaudio.BinauralEffect`](audio.md#binauraleffect-kt-binauraleffect). The placed, binaural output is
[`PatSpatialHeadTrackedDocs`](audio.md#patspatialheadtrackeddocs-kt-patspatialheadtrackeddocs), which needs Steam Audio's `libphonon`
(`./gradlew fetchSteamAudioNatives`).

### What the two clips are for

A single clip of a synth voice makes no claim. These two are the same notation, the same engine
and the same gain, differing only in a **tag that is not a spatial tag**: the second adds `lpf`,
which `patSpatialEventsForArc` forwards to Dough untouched. So everything audible between them
is the forwarding rule, which is the reason to reach for this path over `patSynth`, whose voice
has no `lpf` to forward to.

### The spatial parameters are not in the mono source

Both published clips are peak-normalised, exactly as every other figure in these docs is, so
neither of them can carry a claim about *level*. Three things about this path are measured on
the pre-normalisation buffers instead:

 1. **`pan/0` is a lossless mono tap, not a downmix.** Every event leaves
    `patSpatialEventsForArc` carrying `pan/0`, which puts all of an engine's energy in its left
    channel. The smoke test requires the right channel to peak below `RIGHT_CHANNEL_CEILING`,
    which is what lets [`PatSpatialRoom`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt-patspatialroom) `arraycopy` the left channel rather than compute
    `0.5*(L+R)`, and why the source signal has full amplitude rather than half of it.
 2. **The six spatial tags never reach Dough.** Asserted on the event maps, not on the audio:
    `spat`, `az`, `elev`, `dist`, `occl` and `air` are consumed by this path and `lpf` is not.
 3. **`az` is not in the signal.** The same pattern rendered with `az = 0` and with
    `az = -70` produces a **bit-identical** mono source. The direction lives entirely in the
    effect, which is the part that needs the uncommitted binary.

The third says something about [`DoughEngine`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughengine) as well, and it is what makes these two clips
publishable at all: two engines, separately booted and separately fed, agree to the bit. That is
what [`DocsAudioProvenance`](audio.md#docsaudioprovenance-kt-docsaudioprovenance) requires of any producer, and a wasm runtime does not give it to you
for free — so treat it as a property of this engine rather than of the platform.

## SonicPi.kt { #sonicpi-kt }

Sonic Pi v5 driven from a Field box, in owned mode.

`sonicPi` and `Box.sonicPi` are the box-facing entry points, both booting the one shared
[`SonicPi`](audio.md#sonicpi-kt-sonicpi) on first use. That class carries the control API — running and stopping code, the
mixer, recording, and the log and error feeds that come back into the box. The types around it
model what the daemon sends: [`SonicPiLogMessage`](audio.md#sonicpi-kt-sonicpilogmessage), [`SonicPiError`](audio.md#sonicpi-kt-sonicpierror), [`SonicPiFlash`](audio.md#sonicpi-kt-sonicpiflash),
[`SonicPiPorts`](audio.md#sonicpi-kt-sonicpiports) and [`SonicPiVersion`](audio.md#sonicpi-kt-sonicpiversion).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/SonicPi.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/SonicPi/)

## SonicPiActivity.kt { #sonicpiactivity-kt }

Sonic Pi's per-line activity, shown in the editor.

Sonic Pi tells its client which line just triggered a note — `/flash`, from `play`, `synth`,
`sample`, `control`, `play_chord` and the `with_fx`/`live_loop` block boundaries, tagged with the
caller's line. That answers "what is making sound, and where in the code", so it belongs on the
code rather than in a log.

Three things make this less trivial than painting the lines that flashed.

The rate is musical, not human. Two `live_loop`s at a modest tempo produce something like sixteen
flashes a second and each iteration reports the loop head, the `play` and the `end`. Repainting per
flash would push a decoration set over the websocket faster than anyone can see, so
`sonicPiActivityDecorations` is a pure function of *recency* that a caller samples at a sane rate —
the launch loop's 50ms poll — rather than something the flash handler drives.

Lines have to cool off. A flash is an instant, not a duration, so a line that fired 40ms ago and
one that fired 400ms ago are both "recent" and should not look identical; without a decay the
display latches on and every line that has ever sounded stays lit.

And the line numbers need translating. Sonic Pi counts from line 1 of the source it was handed,
which is the inside of a Kotlin triple-quoted string — see `inferSonicPiLineOffset` for why that
offset is inferred rather than assumed to be zero.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/SonicPiActivity.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/SonicPiActivity/)

## SonicPiEditorExtension.kt { #sonicpieditorextension-kt }

The `#sonicpi` editor extension and the vocabulary it completes against.

Both are static resources rather than strings built here: `sonicpi.js` is served to the browser as
the AMD module `bithero/sonicpi` (see bootstrapMonaco.js) and `sonicpi-vocabulary.json` is fetched
by it at install time. Reading them verbatim is what lets the node-probe smoke test exercise the
code and data that ship, rather than a copy that can drift.

The vocabulary is generated by `tools/generate_sonic_pi_vocabulary.py` from the installed Sonic Pi;
see that script for why it is extracted rather than written.

## SonicPiLaunch.kt { #sonicpilaunch-kt }

The handle Field holds while Sonic Pi is playing, and the registration that ties it to a box's
lifecycle.

`SonicPi.kt` sends the code and returns a [`SonicPiLaunch`](audio.md#sonicpilaunch-kt-sonicpilaunch) naming the Sonic Pi job that resulted;
this file is what makes returning one from a box mean anything. `registerSonicPiLaunchReturnValue`
adds a handler to the return-value registry which runs a coroutine registered as one of the box's
jobs, reports the box as running while Sonic Pi says the job is alive and this launch is still
the box's current one, and stops the job on the way out. That stop runs `NonCancellable`,
because the usual reason for reaching it is that the box was stopped and the stop still has to
get to Sonic Pi.

`awaitJobId` settles which job a launch refers to: it waits for an id
different from the one that was current when the code was sent, so a re-running box cannot
mistake the job it just replaced for its own.

The handler polls the job every 50 ms, which is also the rate the sounding lines are sampled at
to decorate the box while `showActivity` is set.

## SonicPiPatterns.kt { #sonicpipatterns-kt }

Field's pattern algebra as a sequencer for Sonic Pi's engine.

`pat("bd [hh hh] sd")` and the algebra around it (`TidalPatterns.kt`, `PatAlgebra.kt`,
`PatComposition.kt`) keep musical structure exact in rational cycle space and can transform it
live. `SonicPi.kt` owns a real Sonic Pi 5: 66 synths, 42 effects and 206 samples in the installed
vocabulary, and a scheduler better than Field's own. This file is how a pattern reaches that engine
without going through Sonic Pi's own language in a string literal, which the pattern algebra cannot
see into.

There are two routes, good at different things, and both are here.

**compile** — turn a pattern into a Sonic Pi program.

    sonicPiProgram(
        "drums" to pat("bd [hh hh] sd hh"),
        "bass" to pat("<e1 g1> ~ e2 ~").every(4) { it.rev() } on "tb303",
        cps = 0.5,
        cycles = 4
    ).source

gives you a `live_loop` per layer, with `sleep`s that are the pattern's own rational cycle
positions. The result is ordinary Sonic Pi source: paste it into a `#sonicpi` region and edit it by
hand, or hand it to `Box.sonicPiPattern` and hear it. Field's clock is not involved once it is
running — Sonic Pi's scheduler is, which is the accurate one.

The tempo mapping that makes this readable is `SonicPiProgram.bpm`: `use_bpm 60 * cps` makes one Sonic
Pi *beat* exactly one Field *cycle*, so every `sleep` in the emitted program is literally the cycle
fraction the pattern computed. A third stays a third — `Rational(1, 3)` is emitted where a decimal
would round, and a decimal where it would not.

**drive** — Field's clock sequences, Sonic Pi sounds.

    pat("bd*4, [~ cp]*2").sonicPiLive(cps = 0.5)

One `/run-code` per event, dispatched by the same `PatResponseSpec` machinery that drives every
other live pattern in Field, so `.every`, `.degradeBy` and a signal on `gain(...)` stay live while
you edit. Costs a network hop of jitter per note; buys you a pattern you can change mid-bar.

Both return something a box can be running: compile returns a [`SonicPiLaunch`](audio.md#sonicpilaunch-kt-sonicpilaunch), drive returns a
`PatResponseSpec`. Either way the box stays lit while the music plays and stopping the box stops it.

**Atoms become instruments** through [`SonicPiInstruments`](audio.md#sonicpipatterns-kt-sonicpiinstruments), which resolves in this order: an explicit
override, then a real sample name, then a real synth name, then a note (`c4`, `e2`, `60`), then the
drum-machine aliases (`bd`, `sd`, `hh`, `cp`, …). "Real" means *in the installed vocabulary* —
`sonicpi-vocabulary.json`, extracted from the app by `tools/generate_sonic_pi_vocabulary.py`. An atom
that resolves to nothing is reported in `SonicPiProgram.unresolved` rather than dropped, and a
mistyped alias is a test failure rather than silence (`synth.sonic-pi.patterns`).

**Parameters** come from `PatAlgebra`'s annotations, so `with(gain(sine().range(0.2, 0.8)))` works
unchanged. Three of them are not pass-throughs and the difference matters:

- `gain` → `amp:`, unchanged.
- `pan` → `pan:`, rescaled: Field's pan is 0..1, Sonic Pi's is -1..1.
- `cutoff` → `cutoff:` (synths) or `lpf:` (samples), converted: Field's cutoff is **Hz**, Sonic Pi's
  is a **MIDI note number**.

Any other annotation is passed through only if the vocabulary says the target accepts it — `cutoff`
on `:beep` is not a Sonic Pi opt, so it is dropped and recorded in `SonicPiProgram.droppedOpts`
instead of being sent for Sonic Pi to ignore.

Notes are emitted as MIDI numbers, not as `:c4`. Field's `patNoteNumber` defaults a bare `c` to
octave 5 and Sonic Pi's `:c` is octave 4; emitting the number the pattern actually meant removes a
whole class of off-by-an-octave that neither side would report.

## SoundPathMap.kt { #soundpathmap-kt }

Every route Field has from code to something audible, declared — and re-derived from the code.

The counts are the deliverable, so they live here as data rather than in a sentence somebody has
to remember to update: `SOURCE_COUNT` ways to make samples, `SINK_COUNT` ways to get them out of
the process, `INPUT_COUNT` ways to bring them in. Each is one `SoundPath` in `PATHS`, carrying
its role, whether it can run offline, what has to be installed, the symbol it starts at, and the
page that documents it — or `null`, when nothing does. Running this object as a program re-counts
`PATHS` against all four declared totals and fails on disagreement.

The column that decides whether two paths can be used together is `SoundPath.onSeam`. Everything
realtime meets at one signature, `StereoRenderable.render`, which `AudioPatchSpec.Renderer`
repeats character for character. Two paths that both implement it compose for free; a path that
does not implement it composes with nothing. [`SonicPi`](audio.md#sonicpi-kt-sonicpi) is the only one outside it, for a reason no
wrapper reaches: it is a different process, and no sample ever enters this one. What the seam buys
is clear in two earlier arrivals. Behind [`FaustVoiceBank`](synthesis.md#faustpoly-kt-faustvoicebank) are an event scheduler, a voice
allocator and N WebAssembly instances in one GraalVM context, and reaching the speakers, the
visualisers, the Link output and the box lifecycle cost it the five lines of [`FaustPolyNode`](synthesis.md#faustpoly-kt-faustpolynode).
[`PatSynthBank`](patterns.md#patsynth-kt-patsynthbank) is the pattern voice arriving the same way: a scheduler in front of the voice that
already existed, and nothing else.

### Why this is built like [`DocsAudioProvenance`](audio.md#docsaudioprovenance-kt-docsaudioprovenance) and not beside it

[`DocsAudioProvenance`](audio.md#docsaudioprovenance-kt-docsaudioprovenance) guards *published assets*: it scans the docs for `audio=` fences and
re-renders each one. That is the right mechanism for "did a figure rot" and the wrong one for
"did somebody add a path", because a new render path is invisible to it until a page publishes a
clip from it. So this file takes the same three-step shape — declare, derive from the code, fail
on disagreement — and points it at a different derivation: the `MARKERS` are literals that can
only mean "a new way in or out of this process", and every file carrying one has to be
attributed to a declared `SoundPath`.

A marker declares a file-to-path map rather than a bare allowlist because a literal turns up in
the files that *use* a surface as well as in the one that *is* it: `WavFloatArrayWriter.encode`
reaches both the inline-audio sink and its callers, and they belong to different paths. `SELF` is
the sweep's one blind spot, and the audit turns it back into a check by requiring this file to
spell every marker literal, so a literal that has drifted out of the tree cannot sit here
matching nothing.

### Why the fifth marker is the seam itself

The first four markers are all device calls or file writes, and a sample source need be neither.
[`FaustVoiceBank`](synthesis.md#faustpoly-kt-faustvoicebank) — a Faust program played as an instrument by a pattern — carried none of them, so
it sat in the tree undeclared for a month with `SOURCE_COUNT` reading six and the audit green,
which is the one failure this file exists to prevent. The fifth marker is therefore the seam
itself, `override fun generateStereo(`, which every [`StereoNode`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-stereonode) has to spell: a new realtime
stereo source cannot arrive without a hit. It reported two findings on its first run —
[`FaustVoiceBank`](synthesis.md#faustpoly-kt-faustvoicebank), and [`DoughAudioSink`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughaudiosink), which is [`DoughEngine`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughengine) wrapped onto the seam by
`parkDough` and had been declared *off* it since the day this file was written.

What it still cannot see is a source that is off the seam entirely: another [`SonicPi`](audio.md#sonicpi-kt-sonicpi) in another
process, or another whole-buffer free function like `patRenderStereo`. A mono [`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal) is far too
common a literal to mean anything.

## osc.kt { #osc-kt }

OSC in and out, wrapped around JavaOSC (`com.illposed.osc`) and driven from Field's main runloop.
The page that teaches it is `public/docs/osc.md`.

The usual entry points are `osc` and `oscClient`, not the constructors: they hand back cached
[`OscServer`](audio.md#osc-kt-oscserver) / [`OscClient`](audio.md#osc-kt-oscclient) instances (keyed by port, and by host+port) so that re-running a box
during live editing reuses the existing socket instead of rebinding it. [`OscServer`](audio.md#osc-kt-oscserver) binds a UDP
port on every interface (default 9000) in its constructor and starts listening immediately.
Handlers registered with `on` are keyed by OSC address pattern and return a `Generator`. The
handler lambda itself runs on JavaOSC's receive thread when a message arrives; the generator it
returns is started, and resumed once, on the next service pass on the main thread, then resumed
once per pass until it finishes — so a handler can span frames. Every `yield` hands back the
message that started it. [`OscClient`](audio.md#osc-kt-oscclient) opens its outbound socket lazily on first `send`.

Handlers belong to the server, not to the box that registered them: stopping or re-running the
box leaves them in place. Registering the same pattern again replaces the handler; a pattern the
edited code no longer mentions keeps firing until `remove` is called for it.

Three things to know when debugging. A port another program already holds does not make the bind
fail: JavaOSC sets `SO_REUSEADDR`, so both sockets bind and a program bound to `127.0.0.1` takes
what is sent there. A handler that throws is reported as an error on the box that registered it,
and on the console; a failed send is only printed, so a box that sends every frame keeps running.
And [`OscServer`](audio.md#osc-kt-oscserver) has `debug` on by default, printing every incoming message to Field's console
(not to the box).

Constants: `STEP`, `LINEAR`, `SMOOTH`.
